title: Why I #LoveTeaching
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart takes up Gary Abud's #loveteaching social-media campaign, but first argues that it is more than a cute Valentine's Week exercise. Naming what one loves about teaching, he says, works like a 'gratitude push-up' that strengthens the habit of appreciation. He then gives four reasons. The first is the hidden potential in even withdrawn students, pictured through Lewis's Narnian trees and Johnny Appleseed. The second is that the work keeps getting better for teachers who turn their attention from what they cannot control to what they can. The third is the endless room to learn, with a pointed claim that evaluation scores deserve 'a bit' of thought and no more, just as he tells students that grades matter but are not the ultimate thing. The fourth is the joy still available in school: responding to an Atlantic piece on character education gone wrong, he argues that grit and self-control must not crowd out joy, humor, and curiosity, and he rejects the assumptions that assigned texts cannot engage students or that teachers cannot find joy in curriculum they did not write. The piece is a statement of teacher identity: flourishing in a hard era of testing comes from focus, burning questions, and chosen gratitude.
points: Stuart justifies the time spent on a hashtag exercise by treating it as character work: focusing on what you love about teaching is a 'gratitude push-up' that builds a habit of appreciation.
He accepts that the profession is under real strain from testing, curriculum narrowing, and buzzwords, but argues that teachers who narrow their focus to what they can control can still flourish.
His stance on evaluation scores mirrors what he tells students about grades: they give some information and deserve 'a bit' of thought, but keeping his job will not become his top priority.
He proposes 'burning questions' in place of points as the engine of professional growth, crediting the National Writing Project, and lists the questions that drive his own practice.

In response to criticism of joyless character education, he holds that grit and self-control matter alongside joy, humor, and curiosity, and that assigned texts and curriculum a teacher did not write can still hold engagement and joy.
quotes: We teachers don't have enough time in our days; we can't just be doing things like writing #loveteaching posts if it's nothing more than a cute Valentine's Week activity. But it is way more than cute. Gary's idea is solid because the act of focusing on what we love about teaching is like doing a gratitude push-up; it strengthens the mental habit (or character strength) of appreciating what we've got and expressing that appreciation.

A big reason that I love teaching is that there's still this kid in me that thinks potential surrounds us — potential we can't even imagine. I think that even our most broken or withdrawn students can one day, like the Narnian trees, dazzle us. That potential is in them.

By habitually reigning in our focus, turning it from what we can't control to what we can, there's a teacher or two (or more) in every school in the country who is somehow flourishing during even this dark time for the teacher profession. We remind ourselves daily that, while our work is Never Finished, that's not necessarily a bad thing.

I'm the kind of person who doesn't long for a job where you can just be done improving; I don't want that. This is part of the reason I don't fret over evaluation scores and other external measures of my effectiveness. I don't care if I get an A on my evaluation; I do care about whether I've mastered more teaching at the end of this week than I had at the end of last week.

If I tell my students that grades are an important thing in one's life preparation but not the ultimate thing, then I, too, need to live the truth out. Grades do matter in the world we live in, and they can, in some ways, be of use to a learner.

My goodness — just writing those questions makes me want to write thousands more words. This is the good stuff, my friends. Cultivate this drive in yourself that isn't about points, but instead is about questions.

The key for me is always that the baby can't be thrown out with the bathwater. Self-control, grit, perseverance: these things do matter, for both our students and ourselves. Yet joy, humor, unrestrained curiosity — these are important, too.
